work-organization.text: Oceanic exchange required material preparation, shipbuilding, repair and transport. Official reports expose skilled tasks and burdens placed on communities, while a particular wreck and a later jar answer different questions. A cargo route does not establish consent, uniform conditions or every object’s itinerary.

question: How far can a fragment take us?
summary: Silver and manufactured goods crossed the Pacific through a system supported by skilled and coerced work. One wreck, colonial shipbuilding reports and a later Mexican jar make different parts of that history concrete. Their contexts explain some connections while leaving particular makers, labor experiences and object journeys unresolved.

sections.title: Moving goods required several kinds of work
sections.text: The Manila trade joined American silver with Asian manufactured goods, including porcelain and silk. Hecht describes transfers through the Philippines and Acapulco, with some goods staying in the Americas and others crossing Mexico for onward shipment. This was a system of transactions and transport, not a single journey made by every object. Ships also required prepared timber and metalwork. Pineda’s report names people cutting and planing wood, shaping masts and forging nails: useful skills without which a trading connection could not remain afloat.

citations.locator: Short route, cargo and American-market account
Pineda: woodcutters, masters and smiths passages

sections.title: Royal construction placed burdens on communities
sections.text: In 1618 Governor Fajardo reported that royal shipbuilding drew people away from their fields. He described harsh work and contributions from neighbors to support workers whose royal pay was small. Pineda’s separately attributed 1619 report lists different skilled tasks, then describes arrears and people leaving. A stated wage was not necessarily money received. These officials sought changes that would sustain royal service and reduce expense. Their accounts expose burdens without supplying the workers’ own full testimony or establishing identical conditions in every yard and year.

citations.locator: Fajardo: royal shipbuilding; Pineda: pay arrears and flight

sections.title: Follow one interrupted voyage
sections.text: The San Agustín carried Chinese goods from the Philippines toward Mexico in 1595. It wrecked at tamál-húye, present-day Drakes Bay, where Coast Miwok communities already lived. Porcelain recovered in village contexts gives this episode a material setting beyond a captain’s account. The NPS project compares excavation records and written sources while investigating how local people selected and used introduced objects. Proposed practical and ceremonial uses remain interpretations to test, rather than one meaning assigned to every fragment.

Encounter, village archaeology and alternative-use models

sections.title: A later jar is another episode
sections.text: The supplied jar is Mexican tin-glazed earthenware, dated approximately 1680–1700. Its blue and pale decoration includes repeated panels and floral forms. It is not Chinese porcelain or cargo from the 1595 wreck. Hecht uses Mexican ceramics to discuss local responses to imported wares, while the catalogue supplies this jar’s material and date. The picture does not name its potters, buyer or original contents. Comparing it with wreck evidence explains why a known archaeological context can establish connections that an attractive surface alone cannot.

citations.locator: Actual supplied image; Date, Geography and Medium

sections.title: A registered consignment gives a narrower connection
sections.text: Caño Ortigosa and Lee study the Santo Cristo’s 1726 Cavite register for a voyage to Acapulco. Julián Ignacio’s entry joins lacquered furnishings and ceramics described as Japanese with clothing and books. This particular record makes loading and ownership discussable. The authors also warn that declared values omit entries. Registration is evidence for an intended commercial movement, without supplying every good’s actual manufacture, final buyer or successful delivery.

returnPrompt: Why can an excavated fragment establish some connections more securely than a beautiful unprovenanced object?

deeperReading.title: An official’s criticism has a purpose
deeperReading.text: Fajardo contrasts royal construction with smaller private ships, whose workers he describes as paid and consenting. His proposed permission concerns regional navigation, not proof that all Pacific galleon building was voluntary. He also considers buying enslaved people elsewhere for galley service. Criticism of one damaging arrangement therefore does not make the letter a program of freedom for everyone. Pineda similarly writes to the king about preserving the colony and improving royal provision. His technical knowledge and complaints help explain work while leaving the workers’ different aims harder to recover. Both accounts are read here through an old English edition, without an independent check of their Spanish manuscripts.

citations.locator: Fajardo: private/regional ships and proposed galley labor; Pineda heading/purpose

deeperReading.title: A fragment has more than one possible explanation
deeperReading.text: The Tamál-Húye project account reports collaboration with Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria. Its use of several kinds of evidence is valuable without becoming community approval of this atlas. A fragment’s location, wear and association with other objects matter when evaluating possible uses. The project’s models are research questions, not a claim that each imported vessel became a tool or ritual object. The later Mexican jar raises another limit: a collecting record and a photograph are not the same as an excavated wreck association. Keeping those contexts separate makes comparison more informative.

deeperReading.title: A shipping record has its own omissions
deeperReading.text: The Santo Cristo study shows why a declared value cannot automatically measure the entire shipment. Named entries allow a bounded inquiry, while omitted contents, mixed measures and incomplete values limit totals. Original registration and arrival records still need independent comparison.

evidenceReading.title: Separate cargo, working conditions and a later object
evidenceReading.introduction: These are editorial paraphrases. A ship’s documented episode, reports by colonial officials and a museum object each establish different things.

items.label: An excavated fragment has a context to investigate
items.text: The Point Reyes account associates porcelain finds with a 1595 wreck and Coast Miwok village contexts, while keeping a separate Drake-deposit suggestion tentative.
items.interpretation: Context can support a particular connection without recovering every use, owner or cargo item. A proposed ceremonial or practical interpretation is not automatically a demonstrated function for each fragment. The selected Mexican jar is much later.

items.label: A reported wage is not proof of payment or consent
items.text: Pineda identifies skilled tasks and pay schedules but also reports arrears and people leaving. Fajardo describes burdens on royal workers and their communities.
items.interpretation: The complaints expose relationships behind shipbuilding. Their authors serve colonial government, not a neutral survey of workers. Fajardo’s distinction for smaller private regional ships cannot be transferred to every oceanic vessel or taken as proof of enforcement.

items.label: A later Mexican jar is not a recovered shipment
items.text: The supplied photograph shows patterned panels and floral forms. The Met identifies Mexican tin-glazed earthenware, ca. 1680–1700, accession 11.87.36.
items.interpretation: Surface arrangement is observable; date, material and geography use catalogue research. Neither establishes its buyer, original contents or voyage. The date alone prevents putting it aboard the San Agustín in 1595.

familyActivity.title: One jar, two dates and a question about work
steps: Find one repeated panel and a floral form in the supplied jar image. Describe how they fit the curved body without guessing a maker.
Read the source capsule. Make cards for visible observation, catalogue identification and a dated written or archaeological account.
Sort “the panels repeat,” “the jar is Mexican earthenware” and “the San Agustín wrecked in 1595.” Explain why the later jar cannot be that wreck’s cargo.
Write one supported statement about making or movement, then one question about a worker that these records cannot answer.
familyActivity.explanation: Source capsule — editorial paraphrase: the Met identifies this jar as Mexican tin-glazed earthenware, made approximately 1680–1700. The NPS describes a different episode: the San Agustín wrecked in 1595 while travelling from the Philippines toward Mexico. Official reports from 1618 and 1619 describe skilled shipbuilding and burdens on workers and communities. Those reports do not identify this jar’s potters, and its image cannot establish working conditions or a voyage.

review.reviewer: Codex selected source consultation and internal author QA; not independent historian or relevant community approval
review.scope: A wreck episode, translated official work reports, a later Mexican jar and a particular registered consignment. Three selected rereads retain earlier scopes; three new source records keep method, purpose and dates separate. Original case, claims, object order, dimensions and image bytes remain intact.
limitations: Full case 1565–1815, selected reference 1565–1726, wreck 1595, reports 1618/1619, jar ca. 1680–1700 and 1726 consignment are separate. The C7 display edge does not end the trade.

Only selected old English translations were read; no independent Spanish manuscripts, worker petitions, complete cargo manifest or original excavation datasets consulted. Officials’ accounts are not universal labor histories.

The NPS project’s alternative-use models and reported partnership are not all proved outcomes or approval of this atlas. Its update is 2023, not a fresh 2026 field report; the differing 1573 shorthand is excluded.
No new source image, plan, numeric point or precise voyage line adopted. Whole-paper challenges/access failures remain documented without bypass.

The 1726 registration study was read in selected exposed PDF text; page images and original manuscript were not inspected. It is not a delivery receipt, the selected jar’s shipment or a complete quantified trade series.
Independent specialist/community review, real family use, human accessibility/device behavior and physical print acceptance remain open.
